title: Nothing can separate us (Romans 8:31–39)
hookLine: neither death nor life, nor height nor depth
last: A GOOD THREAD IN THE WEAVE.

lines: SOME FEARS COME AS A LIST.
cards: Losing someone. Being alone. Getting sick.
Failing. Being forgotten. Some fears come as a list.
Now suppose a friend on the edge of the bed goes through that list out loud. Naming every one. And after each: no, not even that.
That's what Paul does at the end of Romans chapter eight. After the groaning and the weaving, he lists the worst things he can think of, and lets none of them win.

teach.b: Paul opens with a question, in the King James Bible: "What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?" Paul had plenty of enemies; none of them gets the final say.
Then a list: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?"

In another letter Paul lists his own beatings, hunger, cold and shipwreck, so none of this is abstract to him. And tradition says that Christians in Rome would soon face the sword, and that Paul himself died there.
So his answer isn't cheap: "Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us." Not by escaping them. Through them.
More than conquerors is one word in Greek, a super-conquering.

Then the finale: "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
He builds it in pairs. Death and life: the two ends of everything. Things present and things to come: all of time.
Height and depth: all of space.

teach.h: SHALL BE ABLE TO SEPARATE US FROM THE LOVE OF GOD.
teach.b: Then, in case he's missed anything, nor any other creature. Then he stops. There's nothing left on the list.

how: Romans 8:31–39 is a reading some families choose for Christian funerals, and some Christians memorize verses 38 and 39 to say in times of fear or loss.

o: winning through hardship, not by escaping it
a victory won without ever having to suffer
crushing every enemy so none are left standing

games.q: what's inside the finale — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says those God loves will never face hardship
he lists tribulation, famine and sword, and says "in all these things" we are more than conquerors.
Paul's list is built in pairs
death and life, things present and to come, height and depth: everything.
Paul says nobody will ever be against us
he asks "if God be for us, who can be against us?" enemies are real, but none gets the final say.

games.q: you're Paul, near the end of chapter eight. you've named famine, persecution and the sword. how do you finish?
o: pray that the church in Rome escapes them all.
say that nothing, not even death, can separate us from God's love.
admit some things are stronger than love.
games.why: "neither death, nor life … nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God."

practice: Read verses thirty-eight and thirty-nine slowly from your screen, out loud if you can, in a whisper if you're not alone, pausing after each pair.
When a word touches one of your own fears, stay there for a breath, then read the ending once more: shall be able to separate us from the love of God.
If you pray, let these words be your prayer; if you don't, let them be something you heard said over you.

wordCard.voice: Super-conquering. The one Greek word behind more than conquerors, Paul's answer to his own list of everything that might separate us from God's love.

orig.note: Greek: to separate, to put space between. the verb Paul uses for what nothing can do.

carryVoice: Your line: no, not even that. Not one fear on the list gets the last word. Day three hundred twenty-three, done.
